title: Determinants and Institutions

cards.h: Who decides, and what shapes the decision?
cards.b:
This opening lesson of Paper II Section B asks two simple questions. What shapes India's foreign policy (the determinants)? And who makes it (the institutions)?

The answers explain everything that follows: why India chose non-alignment, why it treats its neighbourhood as a priority, why the PMO and NSA matter so much, and why a state like West Bengal can still block a river deal with Bangladesh.

In the exam, this topic often appears as a general question, such as "Discuss the determinants of India's foreign policy", or it is used as the framework for a longer answer. Prepare a clear list and attach an example to each item.

• Geography: long land borders (about 15,000 km) with seven neighbours, a 7,500 km coastline, and the Indian Ocean on its flank. K.M. Panikkar's India and the Indian Ocean (1945) argued that India's security depends on the seas.
  • History: colonial rule shaped sovereignty, anti-imperialism and sensitivity to outside intervention. Partition made Pakistan a lasting problem.
  • Economy: energy needs, trade, remittances and technology. After 1991 economic interests grew louder.
  • Security: China, Pakistan, terrorism, the nuclear question.

• Ideology and values: Gandhian non-violence, Nehruvian internationalism, and the older ideas of Kautilya (the mandala theory) all appear in Indian thinking. Panchsheel (1954) listed five principles of coexistence.
  • Leadership: Nehru (1947–64) shaped policy personally. Indira Gandhi, Vajpayee, Manmohan Singh and Modi have each left a distinct stamp.
  • Domestic politics: coalition governments (1989–2014) needed consensus; the BJP's majority from 2014 gave the PM freedom. Tamil Nadu (Sri Lanka) and West Bengal (Teesta) play a part. Public opinion and the diaspora matter.
  • International system: the Cold War, then a unipolar moment, now a contested multipolar order.

Scholars: A. Appadorai, The Domestic Roots of India's Foreign Policy (1981); Kanti Bajpai on Nehruvian, neo-liberal and hyper-realist schools of thought.

cards.h: Does India have a strategic culture?
cards.b:
George Tanham (RAND, 1992)

In 'Indian Strategic Thought: An Interpretive Essay', Tanham said India lacked a tradition of strategic planning, because of its fatalism, caste and history of invasions. Indian scholars answered that this was a Western lens.

Kautilya's Arthashastra

The mandala theory: the neighbour is a likely enemy, and the neighbour's neighbour a likely friend. Four methods (saam, daam, dand, bhed). Modern writers such as Shyam Saran (How India Sees the World, 2017) trace links.

Kanti Bajpai

Three schools: Nehruvian (cooperative security), neo-liberal (economics first) and hyper-realist (power, nuclear weapons).

• Article 51 (Directive Principles): the State shall promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encourage settlement of disputes by arbitration.
  • Union List, Seventh Schedule: Entries 10–14 cover foreign affairs, diplomatic and consular matters, the UN, international conferences and treaties. Entry 97 gives residuary powers to the Union.
  • Article 73: the executive power of the Union extends to matters on which Parliament can legislate.
  • Article 253: Parliament can make any law to implement an international treaty, even on a State subject. This is how treaties override the federal division.
  • Article 246 and Article 245: legislative competence.

Importantly, there is no constitutional requirement that Parliament ratify a treaty. The Executive negotiates and ratifies. Parliament's role is mainly to discuss, question and, where needed, legislate.

• In re Berubari Union (1960): the Supreme Court held that Article 3 cannot be used to cede Indian territory. A constitutional amendment under Article 368 is required. The 9th Amendment (1960) followed.
  • Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India (1969): giving away territory (as in the Rann of Kutch award) requires an amendment, but settling a boundary by demarcation does not.
  • Gramophone Co. of India v. Birendra Bahadur Pandey (1984): rules of international law that do not conflict with municipal law are part of Indian law.
  • Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997): the Court used international conventions (CEDAW) to fill a gap in domestic law.

The Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh was implemented by the 100th Amendment (2015) for this reason.

Prime Minister and the PMO

Final authority. The PM sets the broad line and leads summit diplomacy. Modi's personal style is very visible.

External Affairs Minister and the MEA

The Ministry runs missions and negotiations. The Foreign Secretary is its senior career official. The Indian Foreign Service (IFS) was created in 1946.

Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) and the NSA

The National Security Council and the National Security Council Secretariat were set up in 1998. The NSA (Ajit Doval since 2014) coordinates security and has led talks with China as Special Representative.

Others

Defence, Finance and Commerce Ministries; the RAW (1968); ISRO and DAE; the ICCR (1950) for cultural diplomacy; ITEC for training.

• Parliament: question hour, debates and the Standing Committee on External Affairs. The 2008 vote of confidence after the nuclear deal is the biggest case of a foreign policy issue shaking the House. Calls for mandatory parliamentary approval of treaties have been made but not accepted.
  • States: border states shape policy on Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka. The Centre has begun to involve states: for example, through a States Division in the MEA.
  • Think tanks and media: ORF, MP-IDSA, Carnegie India, Gateway House.
  • Business and the diaspora: the diaspora of about 35 million Indians abroad gives soft power and remittances. The Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs was merged into the MEA in 2016.

Critics say India's foreign policy is over-centralised and short of diplomats: its IFS cadre is only about a thousand, small for a state of India's size.

• Geography and security: the 2025 Pahalgam attack and Operation Sindoor; the China border thaw.
  • Economy: response to US tariffs by new FTAs (UK, EFTA, EU).
  • Ideas: multi-alignment as the new label for strategic autonomy.
  • Federal politics: West Bengal's role in the Ganga and Teesta talks with Bangladesh.
  • Leaders: summitry with Putin, Xi, Trump and others, as in Delhi, Tianjin and Washington.

Use such examples to show that the determinants are live and not just textbook headings.

"Discuss the determinants of India's foreign policy." (typical)
"What is the role of the Prime Minister's Office and the NSA in making foreign policy?" (typical)
"Critically examine the role of states in India's foreign policy." (typical)

Structure: (1) intro with a sentence from Nehru's or Jaishankar's view; (2) determinants in two groups (external, domestic) with examples; (3) constitutional basis (Art 51, 253, 73, Union List); (4) institutions and their roles; (5) problems (centralisation, weak parliamentary role, cadre shortage); (6) reforms.

quiz.q: Which Article directs the State to promote international peace and security?
Parliament's power to make laws to implement international treaties comes from:
quiz.w: Article 253 allows legislation even on State subjects.

quiz.q: In re Berubari Union (1960) held that:
o: Cession of territory needs a constitutional amendment
Territory can be ceded under Article 3
quiz.w: Article 3 cannot be used to cede territory; Article 368 is needed.

quiz.q: Which amendment gave effect to the Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh in 2015?
The National Security Council Secretariat was set up in:
Who wrote 'India and the Indian Ocean' (1945)?
The Indian Foreign Service was created in:
Kautilya's mandala theory holds that a neighbouring state is likely to be:
quiz.w: The immediate neighbour is a natural adversary; the neighbour's neighbour a natural friend.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a school identified by Kanti Bajpai?
quiz.w: The three are Nehruvian, neo-liberal and hyper-realist.

quiz.q: Who wrote 'The Domestic Roots of India's Foreign Policy' (1981)?
